Subject: WAN transport options for private VPC (diagram attached)

Hi Karthik,

Thanks again for the walkthrough last week. We've sketched a proposed on-prem -> Redwood Private VPC attachment and wanted your input on the WAN / transport decision before we lock the runbook. Key constraints:

- Primary link is our MPLS to colo; we can provision a public internet backup (SaaS-friendly) or an IPsec/DirectConnect to the cloud provider.
- MTU matters: our fabric strips 50 bytes for MPLS labels, so we expect ~1460 MTU end-to-end.
- Our security team prefers an encrypted tunnel (IPsec) but the network team is pushing for GRE to preserve metadata for telemetry stitching.
- We need a predictable failover sequence and a short test plan (BFD/health checks) for cutover.

Attached is the rough wiring: np-vpc-wiring-03-20.vsdx. Can we get an architectural recommendation focused on:
1) control-plane / data-plane separation for KV cache and telemetry egress,
2) preferred transport (IPsec vs GRE vs provider-peering) and why,
3) MTU & fragmentation mitigations, and
4) a quick validation checklist we can include in the deployment runbook.

We're hoping to schedule a 45-minute call next week to finalize. Proposed window: Thu 3/30 10:00-11:00 PT.

Thanks,

Thomas — thanks for the clear summary and the wiring diagram. High level recommendations below; I'll walk through the tradeoffs on the call but wanted to put these on paper so your stakeholders have something to react to.

TL;DR: Prefer an encrypted L3 tunnel (IPsec or cloud-managed VPN) for primary transport, with GRE as a telemetry/backfill overlay only if you need to preserve on-prem metadata. Avoid GRE-only as the sole transport due to stability and opacity of MTU issues.

Details / reasoning:
- Control plane vs data plane: keep the control plane (control messages, management APIs, leader election hooks) on a separate logical channel that is authenticated and rate-limited. Data-plane (inference traffic, KV cache fetches) should ride the more performant path and be subject to egress proxying and caching. This gives us the ability to throttle/control the control-plane without impacting heavy token flow.

- Transport: IPsec (ESP/AH) or provider-secured peering (if you can do a private/DirectConnect-style link) gives native encryption and predictable MTU behavior. When using IPsec, make sure to account for extra headers (ESP ~50–60 bytes depending on mode) when setting PMTU. If full MTU isn't possible, we recommend MSS/DF handling at the edge plus application-level fragmentation awareness for large artifacts (model shard fetches).

- GRE: use it as an overlay for telemetry tagging (if you need the original on-prem src/dst preserved) or for mirroring non-sensitive flows. GRE will exacerbate MTU fragmentation and makes packet path MTU discovery less reliable. If you do GRE, plan for path-MTU tests and set BFD for rapid failover.

- Health / failover: BFD + active/passive routing is fine for sub-5s failover. The runbook should:
  1) validate IPsec SA establishment,
  2) run MTU probe (1460/1400/1280) and record effective MTU,
  3) test KV cache warmup (load small prompt set and measure 95p latency),
  4) verify observability (token-level tracing) across both control/data planes.

Attachment: I put a short reference brief together (redwood-vpc-reference.pdf) with suggested config knobs for BFD timers, MTU fallback values, and KV cache probe scripts.

We can do Thu 3/30 10:00 PT — that works for Kimberly and me; Marissa will handle the ops/rollout checklist. If that slot is bad for you, propose alternatives.

—Karthik

Thanks Thomas / Karthik — a couple of operational details to call out before the meeting so we don't waste cycles:

- MTU: if your fabric strips 50 bytes, we should design for 1460 minimum. We'll include an explicit step in the runbook to set DF=0 on the tunnel endpoints during cutover and verify TCP MSS clamping at the NAT.
- KV cache warmup: schedule initial warmup runs immediately after BGP/route convergence. We'll provide a small prompt set and expected token latencies per model family; that'll be in the runbook appendix.
- Observability: include a short-lived sampling policy (1%) across the control-plane during initial 24h cutover so we can verify no config drift.
- Fallback policy: prefer route-based failover with BFD and local reaction scripts that pull a low-latency fallback model variant from the nearest region. That avoids routing all traffic over internet backup.

I added two items we'll want to see during the pre-cutover checklist: signed SA config (for IPsec) and a list of allowed egress CIDR ranges for our observability collectors.

Quick ask: Thomas, can you attach your proposed firewall ACLs (ingress/egress) to the thread so we can pre-scan for blocked ports? We typically need TCP 443, UDP 53 (DNS), and a handful of ephemeral for health probes.
